newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets focus on jobs, catch up.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-Australian markets focus on jobs, catch up.

text.p: Australian markets will be playing catchup in early trading this week after Monday's holiday and the strong U.S. labour force report last Friday.

But focus will quickly switch to the domestic situation ahead of Thursday's jobs data for May. Economists will also be watching April housing finance data due to be released on Wednesday for signs of stronger construction activity.
"On the domestic front, housing finance data will tell markets the way ahead while labour market data will wrap up the way it was," Commonwealth Bank economists said in a commentary.
"To this end, April housing finance data will show a strong jump, while an increase in May employment should be enough to suggest that all is not lost on the labour market front."

The bank expects employment to rise by 25,000 - the top end of market expectations. Economists surveyed by Reuters last week forecast on average an unchanged unemployment rate for May of 8.7 percent and a rise in the number of jobs by 13,200.

Weakness in the jobs market has been a key factor in the four interest rate cuts since last July. Economists said a strong increase in housing finance and employment should dampen speculation about a fifth cut anytime soon.
Economists surveyed by Reuters forecast housing finance to rise by an average 10.4 percent after a 1.3 percent fall in March.
AUSTRALIAN BONDS (Fri: 10 yr cash yield 7.33 pct, 3-yr 6.15)
Thursday's labour force report will either push the bond market's two month rally on further, or put a dent in hopes of an easing in monetary policy.
"A rise in total employment of around 25,000 for May would be seen as a negative for debt markets," said Akis Haralabopoulos, chief economist at GIO Australia.
However, if the unemployment rate remains stuck at 8.7 percent, thoughts of an easing in monetary policy are likely to be fuelled.
Before then the market will also see housing finance for April and also has the potential to upset the market's thoughts of a cut in the current 5.5 percent official cash rate.

A large double digit rise is forecast and the focus will be on how much of this is made of the refinancing of mortgages as a figure of this magnitude is likely to spook the market if it consists largely of new financings, given that the data is before last month's mortgage rate cuts.

Speculation of an easing has been simmering in the market since the weak April retail trade report just over a week ago and because of the unusual timing of the May 23 rate cut the market is expected to remain jumpy all week.
The market will start the week with a strong U.S. Treasuries market. The key 30-year bond ended at 6.83 percent on Monday, albeit slightly lower than Friday but holding the gains of last week.

The U.S. unemployment rate fell to the lowest level in nearly 24 years in May but the pace of job growth slowed markedly, the U.S. government said Friday in a report that sparked a powerful rally in financial markets.
The Labor Department said the unemployment rate fell to 4.8 percent in May, the lowest level since October 1973, from April's 4.9 percent.
AUSTRALIAN DOLLAR (Fri: US$0.7591/96, New York 0.7613/18)

For the dollar the outlook is diametrically opposed to bonds since the increased rate risk that would stem from any weakness in the jobs data would give the U.S. dollar an even greater yield advantage.
Offshore investors were discouraged enough by the last easing on May 23 which brought official Australian rates down to U.S. levels for the first time since the early 1980s.
And market rates here were already some way beneath those in the U.S. since investors were anticipating a possible cut here and at least one hike from the Federal Reserve.

The risk of the latter rose somewhat following Friday's U.S. employment report which showed payrolls rose by 138,000 and unemployment fell to its lowest level in more than 23 years in May, although the economic signals were mixed.
Analysts expected local housing finance data would be upbeat enough to help support the dollar but it would prove purely temporary if the jobs numbers were really weak.
In such an event, the dollar was likely to test the 1997 low of US$0.7550 a break of which would return it to levels not seen since February 1996 and open the way to US$0.7450 or even 73 cents.
A rally above resistance at US$0.7630 was needed to relieve the immediate pressure and it would take a break of US$0.7680 to raise the prospect of a trend reversal.
STOCKS (Fri: All Ordinaries 2,600.9, down 3.3 pct)
The Australian share market will look for fresh direction after holding its head above the 2,600 level last week.
The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,600.9, down 9.6 points on a week earlier as the market eased back in moderate trade following strong gains on expectations of a rate cut.
The June share price index futures ended the week holding a 10.1 point premium to the physical market, indicating the positive tone it held all last week remains in place.
Brokers said the market appeared to be less sensitive to overseas movements than in the past and had held up well on Friday with some offshore buying.
"It was a good performance," a Sydney-based broker said.
The market continued to be supported by low interest rates and could kick along further on any evidence of another easing of official interest rates, a broker said.
Wall Street achieved another record closing high on Monday, the second straight day of gains and following the release of U.S. jobs data on Friday. The Dow added 43 points to finish at 7,479.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
